## The curve of the claim {#the-curve-of-the-claim}

```{r}
#| label: spec-curve
#| fig-width: 9.5
#| fig-height: 4.1
# The curve of 64 (data/spec_curve.csv), the chart that the Specification curve
# page draws, with the reference specification tagged in ink. Built on
# curve_base(), so that the next slide reuses this exact panel.
curve_base() +
  mark_layer(dplyr::transmute(curve_ref, tag = "the raw gap of the paper", b_pp, rank, sig))
```

::: {.fs-75}
Every combination of the five decisions that keep more than one option: **`r sum(curve$b_pp < 0)` of `r nrow(curve)`** below zero and **`r sum(curve$b_pp < 0 & curve$sig)`** significant at 5%, from **`r fmt_num(min(curve$b_pp), 1)`** to **`r fmt_num(max(curve$b_pp), 1)`** points; randomisation p at most `r fmt_num(max(curve$p_ri), 4)`.
:::

::: {.src}
data/spec_curve.csv: the height of a mark is the estimate in percentage points, its shape the test of its own model (HC2 *t* for the linear model, *z* for the logit).
:::

::: notes
This is the curve of the claim, the curve drawn on the Specification curve page. Each of the sixty-four marks is a specification, one combination of the five decisions that keep more than one option, ranked from the largest gap on the left to the smallest on the right, and each is a justifiable answer to the claim on these data. Below zero is the direction of the claim, and every mark is below zero and a circle, which means significant at five per cent under the test of its own model, and the randomisation test agrees on every specification. On these data, then, direction and significance are not in dispute, and only the size moves, from twenty points down to twelve, with a visible step in the middle. The tagged mark on the far left is the reference, the raw gap of the paper.
:::

## The published results on the curve {#where-your-result-lands}

```{r}
#| label: spec-overlay
#| fig-width: 9.5
#| fig-height: 4.1
# The same panel with the published result and the five reanalyses
# (data/reference_marks.csv), each placed by its gap in points; the
# published result is tagged "OAs 2017". Marks at the same height share a tag.
curve_base() + mark_layer(marks)
```

::: {.resultline}
The [Specification curve](../curve.html) page draws this curve, with the reference marks and a description of every specification
:::

::: {.src}
data/reference_marks.csv: the published change in predicted probability for the OAs, the workshop's refit of each script for the analysts.
:::

::: notes
The same chart carries six results: the published result of the original authors, tagged OAs 2017, and the five analysts of the robustness study. The published result, UYV3F and P9W8Y sit at the far left, at the raw gap of twenty points, because all three compare the Hispanic with the white names among the replies, and without covariates a logit reproduces the raw gap exactly. EWFMI adds covariates and sits a little to the right, 8PTRZ compares with all the other names and sits in the middle of the left-hand cluster, and 25N5D, which counts every delivered email, sits alone in the right-hand cluster. All six results fall within the range of the curve or at its edge, the two analyses whose choices lie outside the menu, EWFMI and the published model, included, so the spread among the analysts is no wider than the spread among the justifiable specifications.
:::
